title: Design Patterns Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Design Patterns lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Patterns solve repeated problems
entries.summary: A pattern gives a name to a useful design idea. Before choosing one, describe the job the code must do.

example.code:
const job = { input: 3, action: n => n * 2 };
console.log(job.action(job.input));

notes: Adding a pattern without a problem can make simple code harder.

entries.name: Factory functions
entries.summary: A factory makes objects. It keeps object creation in one place so callers do not repeat the setup.

example.code:
function makeBook(title) { return { title, borrowed: false }; }
console.log(makeBook("Moon").borrowed);

notes: Return a fresh object when callers need independent objects.

entries.name: Strategy functions
entries.summary: A strategy is a swappable way to do a job. Pass a function when the rule may change.
notes: Do not hide unrelated side effects inside a strategy function.

entries.name: Observer notifications
entries.summary: An observer listens for a change. The subject tells its listeners when something happens.
notes: Remove listeners when they are no longer needed to avoid repeated work.

entries.name: Adapters translate interfaces
entries.summary: An adapter changes one form of input or output into another. It lets two parts work together without changing both.
notes: Check units before passing a value to another part of a program.

entries.name: Decorators add behaviour
entries.summary: A decorator wraps a function with extra behaviour. The original function can stay focused on its job.
notes: Too many wrappers can hide the order in which work happens.

entries.name: Facades offer a small doorway
entries.summary: A facade gives callers a simple way to use several parts. It hides the order of small steps behind one clear action.
notes: A facade should simplify access, not silently change what the helpers mean.

entries.name: Commands store actions
entries.summary: A command packages an action so it can be saved in a queue and run later.
notes: Saving a command is different from running it.

entries.name: State changes allowed behaviour
entries.summary: State describes the current condition of an object. Different states can allow different actions.
notes: List the allowed state changes instead of accepting every action in every state.

entries.name: Builders collect choices
entries.summary: A builder collects choices before producing a result. It helps when creation has several optional parts.
notes: Do not use a large builder when one short function is clearer.

entries.name: Shared state needs care
entries.summary: A single shared object can be convenient, but every caller sees its changes. This makes hidden links between features.
notes: A shared object is not automatically a good design just because there is only one.

entries.name: Choose the smallest useful design
entries.summary: Compare designs by clarity and the changes you expect. A function, a plain object or a pattern can each be the right choice.

example.code:
const discounts = { none: n => n, half: n => n / 2 };
console.log(discounts.half(12));

notes: Do not force all patterns into one project. Use only the ones that solve a clear need.
